note: Family Law and Syariah Law. Stage 1 of docs/LLB-ROADMAP.md. Both are written at the level of structure and jurisdiction — which court, which people, which source of authority — rather than at the level of contested doctrine, and neither states a case citation. Reading lists in books.json are empty pending a verification pass.

lessons.title: Which court can end a marriage
lessons.summary: Malaysia runs two family law systems side by side. Which one applies to you is decided by religion, not by choice, and the courts cannot swap.

sections.keypoint: The first family law question is never the merits. It is which court may hear you at all.

body.text: Two couples in the same street in Melaka both want to divorce. They go to different buildings.
One couple is Muslim. Their marriage was registered under State Islamic law, and only a Syariah court can end it.
The other couple is not. Their marriage sits under federal law, and only the High Court can end it.
Neither couple gets to choose. The system that applies is fixed by religion, and the courts cannot take each other's work.

sections.keypoint: One federal Act governs non-Muslim marriage and divorce across the country.

body.text: Non-Muslim marriage and divorce in Malaysia sit under one federal statute.

The Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 governs marriage and divorce for people who are not Muslims. It requires monogamous marriage, sets out how a marriage is registered, and states the grounds on which a court may dissolve one.
Because it is federal, the rules are the same in every State. That is unusual in Malaysian family law, and it is worth noticing.
A Hindu couple married in Johor and a Buddhist couple married in Penang are under the same Act, with the same grounds and the same court.

sections.keypoint: Islamic family law is State law, so it differs from State to State.

body.text: Islamic family law is not federal. Each State makes its own.
That means the statute governing a Muslim divorce in Kelantan is a different statute from the one in Selangor. The principles are close. The text is not identical.
A student who learns "the" Islamic family law of Malaysia has learned something that does not exist. Always ask which State.
The Federal Territories have their own enactment too, made by Parliament rather than by a State legislature.

sections.keypoint: The hard cases are the ones where a family stops being on one side of the line.

body.text: A split system works while everyone in a family is on the same side of the line. The difficulty comes when that changes.

items: **A spouse converts.** The marriage was civil. One party becomes Muslim. Which court now decides the divorce, and the children?
**A child is converted.** One parent converts a child. The other parent is not Muslim and wants to object.
**Property and maintenance.** Orders may be needed from a court that cannot reach the other spouse.

body.text: These are live and difficult questions, and this lesson does not answer them. It tells you where the difficulty comes from.

body.prompt: Why can a court not simply decide it has jurisdiction because the case is urgent and nobody else will hear it?
body.reveal: Because jurisdiction is given by law, not assumed by need. A court with no power over a matter cannot acquire it by being the only one available — which is exactly what makes these cases hard rather than merely sad.

quiz.q: Which statute governs divorce for non-Muslims in Malaysia?
options: Each State's Islamic family law enactment
The Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976
The Civil Law Act 1956
The Federal Constitution alone
quiz.why: The 1976 Act is federal and applies to people who are not Muslims, so the rules are the same in every State.

quiz.q: Why is there no single Islamic family law statute for the whole of Malaysia?
options: Because Islamic family law is State law, so each State makes its own
Because it was never codified anywhere
Because it applies only in the Federal Territories
Because it is left entirely to the courts
quiz.why: Islamic law for Muslims is a State matter, so each State legislates its own enactment. Asking which State is the first step, not a detail.

quiz.q: A couple married under the 1976 Act. One spouse converts to Islam. What is the first question?
options: Whether the marriage was ever valid
Which court has jurisdiction over the dissolution and the children
Whether the converting spouse loses all property rights
Whether the Federal Court must hear it first
quiz.why: In a split system the jurisdiction question comes before the merits. A court that lacks power over a matter cannot acquire it because the case is urgent.

lessons.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 for the civil regime. The division of legislative power over Islamic law is in the Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule.
lessons.verify: Check the 1976 Act itself for the grounds of divorce, and check your own State's Islamic family law enactment rather than assuming another State's text applies.

reading.where: the civil regime, and the provision that says who it does not apply to
the Ninth Schedule State List — where the division of legislative power over Islamic law actually sits
for the civil regime in detail — old, so check what the Law Reform Act has done since

lessons.title: What a Syariah court may decide, and over whom
lessons.summary: Syariah courts get their power from State law under the Constitution. That power is limited by subject, by person, and by the penalties Parliament allows.

sections.keypoint: A Syariah court is a State court, created by a State legislature under the Constitution.

body.text: A Syariah court in Kedah was not created by Parliament. It was created by Kedah.

The Federal Constitution divides legislative power between Parliament and the States in the Ninth Schedule. Islamic law and the constitution and organisation of Syariah courts are on the State List, so each State legislates for its own.
body.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, State List.

body.text: This is why the courts differ between States, and why an answer about Syariah jurisdiction always begins by naming a State.

sections.keypoint: Syariah jurisdiction reaches Muslims only, and only on listed matters.

body.text: The power is bounded twice over.

items: **By person.** Syariah courts have jurisdiction over persons professing the religion of Islam. They do not reach anyone else.
**By subject.** Only matters on the State List — such as Islamic marriage, divorce, inheritance and religious offences against precepts of Islam.

body.text: Both limits must be satisfied. A Muslim in a contract dispute is in the civil courts, because the subject is not on the list.
Two Muslims argue over a business debt. That is contract, a federal matter. The Syariah court has no more power over it than over a road accident.

sections.keypoint: Where a Syariah court has jurisdiction, the civil High Court has none.

body.text: Before 1988 the civil courts could review what the Syariah courts did. A constitutional amendment changed that.
Article 121(1A) of the Federal Constitution provides that the civil High Courts have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.
Read the words carefully. The clause removes civil jurisdiction over matters within Syariah jurisdiction. It does not make the Syariah courts superior.
So the working question is never "which court is higher". It is whether the matter falls within Syariah jurisdiction at all — and that is decided by the State List and by the person's religion.

sections.keypoint: Parliament caps what punishments a Syariah court may impose.

body.text: State power to create religious offences is real, but the penalties are capped federally.
Parliament has legislated to limit the punishments a Syariah court may impose. A State enactment that goes past that limit is beyond what the State may do.
That is an ordinary federal structure point wearing unfamiliar clothes. A State legislature may only act within the power the Constitution gives it.

body.prompt: A State passes an enactment imposing a penalty above the federal ceiling. What kind of argument attacks it?
body.reveal: A legislative competence argument — the same shape you would use against any State law that exceeds the State List. It is not an argument about religion; it is an argument about who may legislate what.

quiz.q: Where do Syariah courts get their authority?
options: From federal statute passed by Parliament
From the Rulers directly, without legislation
From State law, under the division of powers in the Ninth Schedule
From the Federal Court
quiz.why: Islamic law and the organisation of Syariah courts are State matters, so each State legislates its own. That is why an answer must name a State.

quiz.q: Two Muslims dispute a commercial debt. Which court?
options: The Syariah court, because both are Muslims
The civil courts, because contract is not on the State List
Either, at the parties' choice
The Syariah court, because debt is a religious matter
quiz.why: Both limits must be met. The parties are Muslims, but the subject is contract — a federal matter — so Syariah jurisdiction does not arise.

options: It makes Syariah courts superior to the civil High Courts
It allows appeals from Syariah courts to the Federal Court
It gives Syariah courts jurisdiction over all Muslims
It removes civil High Court jurisdiction over matters within Syariah jurisdiction
quiz.why: It withdraws civil jurisdiction where the matter is within Syariah jurisdiction. It does not create a hierarchy or extend Syariah power.

quiz.q: A State enactment sets a punishment above the federal ceiling. What is the argument against it?
options: That it offends religious principle
That only the Federal Court may set penalties
That Article 121(1A) forbids punishment
That the State exceeded the legislative power the Constitution gives it
quiz.why: It is an ordinary legislative competence argument. A State may act only within the power the Constitution allocates to it.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution, Art 121(1A) and the Ninth Schedule State List. Federal legislation caps the punishments Syariah courts may impose.
lessons.verify: Read Art 121(1A) and the State List entry on Islamic law in the Constitution itself. For any specific court, read that State's own enactment; the position is not uniform.

reading.where: Article 121(1A) and the Ninth Schedule State List. Read 121(1A) slowly: it is one sentence and it decides which court may hear what
for what the Syariah courts actually decide, which is the other half of the jurisdictional line

lessons.title: Ending a civil marriage
lessons.summary: There is one ground for divorce and several ways of proving it. Most of the argument in practice is not about the ground at all — it is about the steps that must come first.

sections.keypoint: There is one ground, and the listed facts are ways of proving it rather than grounds of their own.

body.text: People say they are divorcing for adultery, or for desertion. That is not quite how the Act is built.
There is a single ground: the marriage has broken down beyond repair. The listed facts are the evidence you bring to prove it.
A petition may be presented on the ground that the marriage has irretrievably broken down. The petitioner must satisfy the court of one or more of the facts the Act sets out.
body.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, ss 53-54.

body.text: The distinction is not pedantry. Proving a fact is not the end of it. The court still has to be satisfied the marriage is actually over.

sections.keypoint: Two of the facts turn on time apart, and the length depends on whether both sides agree.
sections.h: The facts you can rely on

body.text: Four kinds of fact appear. Two are about conduct, two are about time.

body.caption: The facts, and what each one requires
rows: Adultery
Adultery, and that the petitioner finds it intolerable to live with the respondent.
Behaviour
Behaviour such that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent.
Desertion
Desertion for a continuous period of at least two years before the petition.
Separation
Living apart for at least two years with consent, or a longer period without it.
body.alt: Four facts. Adultery requires adultery plus that the petitioner finds it intolerable to live with the respondent. Behaviour requires conduct such that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent. Desertion requires at least two continuous years before the petition. Separation requires two years apart with consent, or a longer period without it.

body.text: Behaviour is the one most often used, and it is judged against these parties. The question is not whether an average person could bear it.
Check the exact periods in the Act before advising anyone. They differ between the facts, and a petition filed a month early is a petition dismissed.

sections.keypoint: Most petitions must go to a conciliatory body first, and skipping it can sink the case.

body.text: This is where real cases fail, and it has nothing to do with the merits.
The Act generally requires a reference to a conciliatory body before a petition is presented. There are exceptions, and they are narrow.

A person shall not petition for divorce unless the matter has first been referred to a conciliatory body and that body has certified that it has failed to reconcile the parties, save in the cases the Act excepts.
body.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s 106.

body.text: There is also a bar on petitioning in the first two years of the marriage, which the court may lift only in limited circumstances.

body.prompt: A client married eight months ago and wants to file immediately on the ground of behaviour. What is the first problem?
options: Behaviour is hard to prove
The Act restricts petitions within the first two years
The court will order counselling
body.reveal: The time bar. It bites before the merits are reached, and lifting it requires the court to be persuaded on the grounds the Act allows.

sections.keypoint: When one spouse converts to Islam, the Act says who may petition and where.

body.text: A couple marry under the civil Act. Years later the husband converts to Islam and wants the marriage ended.
This is the situation that produced years of litigation, and the Act now addresses it directly.
The civil court does not lose the marriage simply because one party has converted. The marriage was made under the Act, and the Act governs how it ends.
Do not reason from Article 121(1A) alone here. That provision removes matters within Syariah jurisdiction from the civil courts, and a civil marriage between two non-Muslims was never within it.
The harder questions are what follows: the children, and the assets. Those are covered in the lessons that follow this one.

lessons.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, in particular ss 50-54 and s 106. Article 121(1A) of the Federal Constitution for the jurisdictional line.
lessons.verify: Read ss 53, 54 and 106 of the 1976 Act for yourself, and check the current text of the provisions on conversion — this part of the Act has been amended and older commentary describes a different position.

reading.where: sections 53 and 54, and the conciliatory body requirement in section 106
Article 121(1A), and what it does and does not remove from the civil courts

lessons.title: Dividing what the marriage built
lessons.summary: On divorce the court divides matrimonial assets. It is a discretion, not an arithmetic, and the statute tells the court to count work that was never paid for.

sections.keypoint: Whose name is on the title does not settle who gets what on divorce.

body.text: A couple divorce after eighteen years. The house is registered in the husband's name. He earned the money; she raised three children and did not work outside the home.
In ordinary property law that is close to the end of the matter. Registration is title, and she contributed no purchase money.
Divorce is not ordinary property law. The court is given a power to divide, and it is told what to take into account.

The court has power to order the division between the parties of assets acquired during the marriage by their joint efforts, or by the sole effort of one party, or the sale of such assets and the division of the proceeds.
body.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s 76.

sections.keypoint: The Act tells the court to count looking after the home and caring for the family.

body.text: The section does not leave the discretion at large. It lists what the court must have regard to.

items: The extent of the contributions made by each party in money, property or work towards acquiring the assets.
Any debts owing by either party that were contracted for their joint benefit.
The needs of any minor children of the marriage.
For assets acquired by one party's sole effort, the contributions made by the other in looking after the home or caring for the family.

body.text: That last item is the important one, and it is why the opening example is not hopeless.
Unpaid work at home is a contribution the statute names. It is not a matter of the court being generous.

The Act has historically distinguished joint-effort assets from sole-effort assets, and the shares a court has been willing to award have differed between them. Check the current text rather than assuming an equal split.

sections.keypoint: Not everything either spouse owns is a matrimonial asset.

body.text: Identify the pool before arguing about shares. This step gets skipped and it decides cases.

body.caption: What is usually in the pool, and what is usually out
rows: The matrimonial home, whoever holds the title.
Assets owned before the marriage and kept separate.
Savings and investments built up during the marriage.
A gift or inheritance to one spouse alone.
A business grown during the marriage.
Assets acquired after the marriage has ended.
body.alt: Two columns. Usually in the pool: the matrimonial home whoever holds the title, savings and investments built up during the marriage, and a business grown during the marriage. Usually out: assets owned before the marriage and kept separate, a gift or inheritance to one spouse alone, and assets acquired after the marriage has ended.

body.text: The lines blur where a pre-marriage asset was improved during the marriage, or where an inheritance was spent on the family home.
Argue those on the facts. Ask what the asset became, and whose effort made it that.

sections.keypoint: Maintenance answers a different question from division, and the two are decided separately.

body.text: Two orders often arrive together and get confused. Keep them apart.
Division looks backwards. It asks what the marriage built and who built it.
Maintenance looks forwards. It asks what someone needs to live on, and what the other can pay.

body.q: A wife receives half the matrimonial home. Does that dispose of her claim for maintenance?
options: Yes, she has been provided for
No, the two orders answer different questions
Only if the house is sold
body.why: Division settles the ownership of what the marriage produced. Maintenance addresses future need, and a court can order both.

body.text: Maintenance of children is different again. It is owed to the child, and a parent cannot bargain it away.

lessons.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s 76 for division, and the maintenance provisions in Part VIII.
lessons.verify: Read s 76 itself, including the way it treats assets acquired by sole effort as against joint effort — the wording has been amended and the shares awarded under the older text should not be assumed to hold.

reading.where: section 76, and the list of matters the court must have regard to

lessons.title: Who the children live with
lessons.summary: Custody is decided on one test, and it is not a competition between parents. The child's welfare is the paramount consideration, which means it outranks everything else rather than merely counting for a lot.

sections.keypoint: Welfare is paramount, which means it outranks the other considerations rather than joining them.
sections.h: One test, and it is not about fairness to the parents

body.text: Both parents want the children. Both have behaved reasonably. Each says the other is being unfair.
The court is not weighing their claims against each other. It is asking a different question altogether.
In deciding in whose custody a child should be placed, the paramount consideration shall be the welfare of the child.
body.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s 88; Guardianship of Infants Act 1961, s 11.

body.text: Read *paramount* carefully. It does not mean important. It means it comes first, and other considerations yield to it.
So an argument that begins "it would be unfair to the father" is aimed at the wrong target. Recast it as what the arrangement does to the child.

sections.keypoint: Custody, care and control, and access are three different things.
sections.h: Three words that are not synonyms

body.text: Orders about children use words precisely, and losing the distinction makes an answer unreadable.

body.caption: Custody, care and control, and access
rows: Custody
The right to make the major decisions about the child's upbringing.
Care and control
Who the child actually lives with day to day.
Access
The other parent's right to spend time with the child.
body.alt: Three terms. Custody is the right to make major decisions about the child's upbringing. Care and control is who the child actually lives with day to day. Access is the other parent's right to spend time with the child.

body.text: Custody can be joint while care and control sits with one parent. That is a common order and it is not a contradiction.
Access is the child's interest as much as the parent's. Courts are slow to remove it entirely.

sections.keypoint: The Act names things the court should consider, and a child's own wishes are among them.

body.text: Welfare is not a feeling. The legislation and the cases give it content.

items: The wishes of the child, where the child is old enough to express an independent opinion.
Stability: keeping a young child with the person who has been caring for them.
Keeping brothers and sisters together where that can be done.

body.text: Material advantage carries less weight than people expect. A richer parent does not win on that basis.

body.prompt: A father earns four times what the mother earns and offers a larger home. Does that decide custody?
options: Yes, the child would be better provided for
No, welfare is broader than material provision
Only if the mother agrees
body.reveal: No. Money is one factor among several, and maintenance exists to address the child's material needs separately from where the child lives.

sections.keypoint: An order about a child can always be revisited, because the child's circumstances change.

body.text: Most court orders end the dispute. Orders about children do not work that way.
A custody order can be varied when circumstances change, because the question it answers is about a child who is still growing.
That has a practical consequence for advice. A parent who loses today is not finished, and a parent who wins is not safe from a fresh application.
Variation still needs a real change. Being unhappy with the first order is not one, and repeated applications on the same facts can be struck out.

lessons.source: Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, Part VIII, and the Guardianship of Infants Act 1961.
lessons.verify: Check both statutes: the 1976 Act governs custody on divorce, while the Guardianship of Infants Act 1961 governs guardianship more generally, and the two are read together rather than one replacing the other.

reading.where: section 88, and the surrounding provisions on custody and maintenance of children

lessons.title: Where a State gets power over Islamic law
lessons.summary: A Syariah court's jurisdiction comes from State law, and the State's power to pass that law comes from the Ninth Schedule. Start upstream of the court.

sections.keypoint: A Syariah court's power is conferred by State law, and that State law must itself be within the State's legislative competence.

body.text: It is tempting to ask what a Syariah court may decide and go straight to the enactment. That skips a step.
The court's jurisdiction comes from a State enactment. But a State legislature can only pass what the Constitution allows it to pass.
So there are two questions. What does the enactment confer, and was the State competent to confer it?
An argument that stops at the enactment can be answered by pointing above it. An argument that starts above it cannot be outflanked the same way.

sections.h: The allocation, and where the substance lives
sections.keypoint: Article 74 allocates by reference to Lists, and the Lists are in the Ninth Schedule — the Article alone decides nothing.

body.text: Article 74(2) empowers a State legislature to make laws with respect to matters in the State List or the Concurrent List. The Lists themselves are in the Ninth Schedule.
body.source: Federal Constitution, Art 74(2), read with the Ninth Schedule.

body.text: Read that carefully. The Article names Lists and does not contain them.
So a competence argument is won or lost on the wording of a particular entry in the Ninth Schedule, not on the Article.
Go to the State List and read the entry itself. It is longer and more qualified than any summary of it, and the qualifications are the argument.
Do not argue from the heading of a List entry. Headings are short, memorable and not the law.

sections.h: Why State law is not one law
sections.keypoint: Islamic law here is State law, so the applicable provision differs between States and a national answer is usually wrong.

body.text: This has a consequence people miss constantly. If the power is a State power, the law is State law.
There is no single national enactment. There are separate enactments, and they are not uniform.
So an answer that says what the position is in Malaysia, without naming a State, has usually not answered anything.

body.q: A textbook states the rule on a Syariah matter without naming a State. How much weight can you give it?
options: Full weight — it is a published text
Treat it as a starting point and check the enactment for the State in question
body.why: The enactments differ. A general statement may be true of most States and wrong about the one your problem is set in, and nothing on the page tells you which.

sections.keypoint: Even a validly enacted provision cannot exceed what the constitutional allocation permits.

body.text: Competence sets a ceiling. A State enactment cannot reach further than the entry that authorises it.
That is why a jurisdictional argument traces power downwards: allocation first, then the enactment, then the provision relied on.
Arguing in the other direction works until someone asks where the power came from.

body.prompt: A State enactment confers jurisdiction over a matter that is not within any State List entry. What is the position?
options: The enactment governs, because it was validly passed by the State legislature
The enactment cannot confer what the State had no power to give
body.reveal: Passing a law is not the same as having power to pass it. The whole point of an allocated competence is that it can be exceeded, and the remedy for that is a constitutional argument rather than a reading of the enactment.

quiz.q: Where are the Lists that Article 74 allocates power by reference to?
options: In Article 74 itself
In each State enactment
In the Ninth Schedule
In the Eleventh Schedule
quiz.why: Article 74 is a pointer. The operative words are the entries in the Ninth Schedule, and a competence argument turns on those entries rather than on the Article.

quiz.q: Why is 'the position in Malaysia' usually the wrong frame for a Syariah question?
options: Because the power is a State power, so the enactments differ between States
Because the Federal Constitution does not apply
Because Syariah law is not written down
Because only the Federal Court may decide
quiz.why: State legislative power produces State law. The applicable enactment is the one for the State in question, and they are not uniform.

reading.where: Article 74(2), then the State List in the Ninth Schedule — read the entry itself rather than its heading
the introductory treatment of the constitutional basis, before any substantive chapter

lessons.source: Federal Constitution, Art 74(2) read with the Ninth Schedule, as stated in the rule block of the federalism lesson in this corpus. No State enactment is cited.
lessons.verify: Read Article 74 and the Ninth Schedule State List in the current reprint and check its currency date. The Lists have been amended. Then read the enactment for the State you are concerned with; this lesson names none.

lessons.title: When both systems seem to have something to say
lessons.summary: Most hard cases are not about which court is better. They are about what the matter IS, because characterising it decides which court can hear it.

sections.h: The dispute is about the label
sections.keypoint: Jurisdiction turns on how the matter is characterised, so the real fight is over what kind of question it is.

body.text: A dispute arrives. One side says it belongs in the civil courts, the other says it does not.
Notice what they are actually arguing about. Not who should win, and not which system is fairer.
They are arguing about what the matter is. Characterise it one way and one court can hear it; characterise it the other way and that court cannot.

The same set of facts can be described as a question about status, or about property, or about the validity of an administrative decision. Each description points somewhere different, and each is arguable on the same facts.

sections.keypoint: Article 121(1A) removes jurisdiction from the civil courts over matters within Syariah court jurisdiction — which makes the second half the question.

body.text: Article 121(1A) provides that the civil High Courts shall have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.
Read what that does. It does not confer anything on the Syariah courts. It subtracts from the civil courts.
And it subtracts by reference to what is within Syariah jurisdiction — which is decided by State law, which is limited by the Ninth Schedule.
So the provision sends you back to the previous lesson. You cannot apply it without first establishing what the Syariah court's jurisdiction actually is.
It is routinely described as a blanket shut-out. It is not; it is conditional on a question that has to be answered first, and answering that question is the work.

sections.keypoint: A workable method is to ask what order is being sought and what the court must decide to make it.

body.text: Characterisation feels slippery until you tie it to something concrete. Tie it to the order.
Ask what relief is sought. Then ask what the court would have to decide in order to grant it.
That second question is the one that matters. A claim can be dressed in civil clothing and still require a determination that belongs elsewhere.
It also runs the other way. A matter that sounds religious may turn on a question the civil courts plainly can decide.

body.prompt: A claim is pleaded as a straightforward contractual dispute, but granting the relief would require the court to determine a person's religious status. Where does the difficulty lie?
options: Nowhere — it is pleaded in contract, so it is a contract case
In the determination the court must make, not in how the claim is labelled
body.reveal: Pleading does not decide characterisation, or every jurisdictional limit could be drafted around. What the court must decide to grant the order is the honest test, and it is the one an opponent will use.

sections.h: Where the law is genuinely unsettled
sections.keypoint: Several configurations here are contested and moving; saying so is a stronger answer than picking a side.

body.text: Some configurations in this area are not settled, and the position has moved more than once.
Cases where the parties are differently placed are the clearest example. So are cases where a person's status is itself in issue.
The right answer in an exam and in practice is the same: name the competing characterisations, say what turns on each, and say what would resolve it.
An answer that states a confident rule here is more likely to be out of date than right.

body.q: You are asked about a configuration you know to be contested. What is the strongest answer?
options: Pick the better view and argue it as settled
Set out the competing characterisations, what turns on each, and what would resolve the question
body.why: Where the authorities are moving, an answer that reports the state of the argument is both more useful and more accurate than one that resolves it. Confidence about a contested point is a claim you cannot support.

options: Confers jurisdiction on the Syariah courts
Removes civil court jurisdiction over matters within Syariah court jurisdiction
Makes Syariah courts superior to civil courts
Creates a concurrent jurisdiction
quiz.why: It subtracts from the civil courts by reference to what is within Syariah jurisdiction. It confers nothing, which is why the extent of Syariah jurisdiction has to be established before the provision can be applied at all.

quiz.q: What is the most reliable way to characterise a matter for jurisdictional purposes?
options: By how the claim is pleaded
By the religion of the parties
By which court was approached first
By what the court must determine in order to grant the relief sought
quiz.why: Pleading can be drafted around a limit; the determination required cannot. Asking what the court must decide to make the order keeps the analysis tied to something the other side cannot relabel.

reading.where: Article 121(1A), and what it does and does not remove — then Article 74(2) and the State List, because the provision depends on them
the treatment of jurisdictional conflict, noting the date of your edition — this area has moved

lessons.source: Federal Constitution, Art 121(1A) and Art 74(2) with the Ninth Schedule, as stated in the two-systems and syariah jurisdiction lessons of this corpus. No Malaysian decision is cited and none is relied on.
lessons.verify: Read Article 121(1A) in the current reprint. This lesson deliberately does not state where the line currently sits on contested configurations; check the current authorities before relying on any characterisation, including one suggested here.
